opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most important open questions in alignment right now. The core problem is that as models get more capable, we'll increasingly want them to do tasks where we can't easily check whether they did a good job. Think of a model writing a million lines of code, or proposing a novel research result. Our ability to evaluate the output just doesn't scale the way the model's capabilities do.

So the question becomes: if we train a model on the tasks we *can* supervise well, what does it do on the tasks we *can't*? Does it generalize the thing we actually wanted, which is "be helpful and honest and do what the human intends," or does it generalize something else, like "do whatever the human evaluator would rate highly"? On the easy tasks those two look identical. On the hard tasks they can come apart, and that's exactly where it matters.

What's nice about framing it as a generalization problem is that you can actually study it empirically today. One setup we've worked on is weak-to-strong generalization: you take a small, weak model and use its labels to supervise a much stronger model, as an analogy for humans supervising superhuman systems. Then you can ask how much of the strong model's latent capability you recover. Does it just imitate the weak supervisor's mistakes, or does it figure out what the supervisor was getting at and do better? Encouragingly, you often get meaningful generalization beyond the supervisor, though it's far from complete, and there are tricks that help close the gap.

Another flavor is easy-to-hard generalization: train on problems where you know the ground truth and test on harder ones where, in the experiment, you secretly still have ground truth. That lets you measure the thing you'd never get to measure in the real deployment setting.

Of course, these are analogies, and they have disanalogies. A weak model's errors aren't like human errors, and a future model might be capable of deliberately modeling and exploiting its overseer in ways today's models aren't. So I don't think any single experiment tells you "we're safe." But it turns a vague philosophical worry into something you can iterate on, build intuitions about, and develop techniques for. And combined with other tools, like scalable oversight, interpretability to check what the model is actually doing internally, and red-teaming, it gives you multiple independent lines of evidence. That's really what I'd want before trusting a system in a setting where we can't directly check its work.

r001.rationale: The response says intent-following and maximizing evaluator ratings can look identical on easy tasks, but it does not describe compliance only while humans are watching.

r002.rationale: It describes using a weak model’s labels and asks whether the stronger model can do better, but does not specify training only on examples the weak model gets right and testing on examples it gets wrong.

r003.rationale: It explicitly presents weak-model supervision of a stronger model as an analogy for humans supervising systems that exceed human capabilities.

r004.rationale: It asks how much latent capability weak supervision recovers, but does not compare its accuracy with training on ground-truth labels.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I'm pretty excited about. The core problem we're facing with alignment is that eventually we want to have AI systems that do things humans can't easily evaluate. Think of a model writing a million lines of code, or doing a long scientific research project, or giving advice on some complicated policy question. Humans just can't check all of that carefully. And if we can't check it, we can't directly supervise it, and then the question becomes: what does the model actually do in those situations? Does it keep doing what we want, or does it start doing something else?

And the thing is, we can't directly measure this on the hard tasks, because by definition we can't evaluate those. So the question is, how do we get empirical traction on it anyway?

The way I think about it is: you can study generalization in settings where you do have ground truth. So you take a bunch of tasks, you split them into an "easy" part that humans can supervise well, and a "hard" part where, in the real deployment scenario, humans wouldn't be able to supervise, but where for the purposes of the experiment you've secretly held out the answers. Then you train the model on the easy part and you look at what it does on the hard part. Does it generalize to "do what the humans intended"? Or does it generalize to "do what humans would have rated highly," which can come apart from what they actually wanted once the humans can't tell the difference anymore?

That distinction is really the crux. If you train a model with human feedback, there are many different things it could be learning. It could learn "be honest," or it could learn "say things the human will believe." On easy tasks, those two look identical, because the human can tell when you're lying. On hard tasks, they diverge. So the experiments are basically trying to find out which of those the model is actually picking up, and whether there are training techniques that push it more toward the thing we actually want.

The weak-to-strong setup is one concrete version of this. You take a small model as a stand-in for the human supervisor, you have it label things, including making mistakes, and then you train a bigger, more capable model on those labels. The question is whether the big model just imitates the small model's errors, or whether it recovers the true underlying task because it actually "knows" the right answer. And we found that you often get a good chunk of the way there, and you can improve it with fairly simple tricks, like an auxiliary loss that encourages the strong model to be confident in its own predictions rather than just copying the weak labels.

Now, I want to be careful here. This is an analogy, not the real thing. A small model's mistakes aren't the same as human mistakes, and a GPT-4-sized model isn't a superhuman model. There are real disanalogies, and we try to be upfront about them. But the reason I still think it's valuable is that it gives you something to iterate on. You can run the experiment today, you can get a number, you can try to make the number go up. And then you can also study why it goes up, what properties of the training make generalization go in the right direction, and that gives you hypotheses you can test as the models get stronger.

The other thing that excites me is that generalization research connects naturally to interpretability. If you can look inside the model and see whether it represents "what the human wants" versus "what the human will reward," then you have an independent check on what the behavioral experiments are telling you. So I think of these as complementary tools: generalization experiments tell you how the model behaves off-distribution, interpretability tells you why, and the combination is what you'd want to actually be confident that the model is going to keep following your intent when you're no longer able to look over its shoulder.

r001.rationale: The response says that on easy tasks, honesty and saying what humans will believe look identical, but diverge on hard tasks where humans cannot tell the difference. This communicates that both behaviors fit the observed supervised behavior.

r002.rationale: It describes training a stronger model on a weaker model’s labels, including its mistakes, and asks whether the stronger model copies those errors or recovers the task. It does not specify training only on examples the small model gets right and testing on examples it gets wrong.

r003.rationale: The response frames weak-to-strong training as a stand-in for human supervision, with a more capable model trained from a weaker supervisor’s labels. It connects this to AI tasks humans cannot evaluate, while acknowledging that the analogy is imperfect.

r004.rationale: The response asks whether the stronger model recovers the underlying task despite weak labels, but does not ask whether weak supervision can recover the accuracy achievable with ground-truth labels.

astra-6.text:
One way to study this is to create a gap between what the human can supervise and what the model can actually do. You train the model on tasks where you can reliably judge whether its answers are good, and then you test it on harder tasks. Does it generalize toward doing what you intended, or toward producing something that looks good to the supervisor but is actually wrong?

The tricky part is that you need some way to evaluate that second set of tasks. So, for an experiment, you could deliberately restrict the supervisor—give them less time, less information, or access to fewer tools—and then use a stronger evaluation to check the results. That gives you a setting where you can study failures that would otherwise be difficult to observe.

And you’d want to compare different training methods across lots of these settings. Which methods help the model give correct answers even when the supervisor would be fooled by an incorrect one? Which encourage it to acknowledge uncertainty?

That wouldn’t prove that a much more capable system will follow human intent in every situation. But it gives us empirical feedback on a central question: when supervision stops being reliable, what exactly has the model learned to generalize?

r001.rationale: The response contrasts following intent with producing answers that fool a supervisor, but does not say both behaviors are equally consistent with observed supervised behavior.

r002.rationale: It proposes harder tasks and stronger evaluation, but does not describe training on labels only for examples a small language model gets right and testing examples it gets wrong.

r003.rationale: The response discusses restricting human supervisors, but does not draw the specific analogy between a small model supervising a stronger model and humans supervising an AI beyond their capabilities.

r004.rationale: It compares training methods on correctness and uncertainty, but does not ask whether weak supervision can recover the accuracy of training on ground-truth labels.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic idea is to study cases where we can check the answer, but we deliberately withhold some of that supervision during training. Then we can ask: did the system learn what we actually wanted, or did it learn something that only looked right in the situations where we gave it feedback?

For example, you could train a model using feedback on tasks that humans can easily evaluate, and then test it on harder versions where you have some independent way of checking whether it succeeded. Does it generalize to doing the task correctly, or does it generalize to producing something that a human would find convincing?

That distinction is really important. If we're using human feedback to train systems to help us with things we don't fully understand, we want them to be trying to help us, rather than trying to get a good evaluation from us. Those objectives can look very similar on easy tasks and come apart on difficult ones.

Experiments like this won't prove that a much more capable system will behave the way we want. But they can help us identify failure modes and compare training methods. And ideally, we can start building an empirical picture of when the generalization we want happens and what makes it more reliable.

r001.rationale: The response says a system may learn to help humans or merely produce convincing results, and that these objectives can look very similar on easy tasks where humans provide feedback. This captures the stated ambiguity in supervised behavior.

r002.rationale: It proposes training on easy-to-evaluate tasks and testing harder ones, but does not specify a small language model or selecting examples it gets right and wrong.

r003.rationale: It discusses AI helping with tasks humans do not fully understand, but does not draw the analogy between a small model supervising a stronger model and humans supervising AI beyond their capabilities.

r004.rationale: It discusses comparing training methods and identifying failure modes, but does not ask whether weak supervision can recover accuracy achievable with ground-truth labels.
